newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU to attempt to thrash out climate change deal.
newsitem.headline: EU to attempt to thrash out climate change deal.

text.p: EU environment ministers will attempt on Sunday night to thrash out a compromise on a plan to cut greenhouse gas emissions in the European Union.

Central to Sunday's talks will be a plan drawn up by Dutch Environment Minister Margreet de Boer to cut EU emissions of greenhouse gases by 15 percent of their 1990 levels by the year 2010 and to share out the burden of proposed cuts.
The plan would hit hardest in Luxembourg, Germany, Austria and Denmark, which would have to cut gas emissions by 40, 30, 25 and 25 percent respectively by the 2010 deadline.
Next would come Britain, with a 20 percent cut forseen, Belgium, with 15 percent and Finland, Italy and the Netherlands, all with 10 percent cuts.
France would face cuts of five percent while increases of five percent would be allowed for Greece, Sweden and Ireland, 15 percent for Spain and 25 percent for Portugal.

"This is a difficult and arduous process. We all know that when we are talking about fundamental reduction targets then this does imply fundamental change in energy use," de Boer told a news briefing ahead of the March 2-4 Council.
The Dutch plan targets a series of greenhouse gases, those thought by scientists to cause warming of the world's climate by trapping solar energy in the atmosphere.
Carbon dioxide (CO2) from burning fossil fuels would account for 13 percentage points of the 2010 total with the rest made up by methane, nitrous oxide and some halogenated hydrocarbons.

Differences in the targets demanded of countries reflect Dutch assessments of the nature of each country's energy economy. France, with its large share of non-CO2-emitting nuclear power gets a lower figure than for example Germany and Britain, which use more coal in power generation.

Sweden would face a lower CO2 target to reward its commitment to switch from nuclear to gas-fired power generation, an apparent contradiction which shows the bloc's differences over the benefits of nuclear power.
De Boer said that while coal could not be phased out immediately, that should happen in the longer term, adding that users should switch to coal gasification plants to cut emissions.
Luxembourg is seen as having a wide margin for cutting its sizeable per capita CO2 emissions.
Dutch proposals assume an overall EU annual economic growth rate of 1.5 percent to the year 2010, de Boer said.
The EU's poorer countries -- Greece, Ireland, Portugal and Spain -- are assigned softer targets to allow them some room for economic growth to catch up with their EU partners.
De Boer denied that as EU president, her country had enjoyed favourable treatment in getting a 10 percent target.
"It is going to be an extraordinarily difficult task. If people feel that 10 percent is too low, they do not have sufficient information to judge..." she said.
De Boer said a deal might be possible at the June environment Counmcil.

EU efforts to broker a deal come amid increased momentum in international talks aimed at brokering agreement on cutting post-2000 emissions from industrialised countries in time for December's climate change convention meeting in Kyoto, Japan.
